questions.question: A company runs 1,200 Linux and Windows VMs across 30 projects. It needs to apply OS security patches on a recurring schedule during maintenance windows, and to report which VMs are missing patches. What should the engineer use?
options: Run `apt upgrade` from startup scripts on every boot of the VMs.
Recreate the machine images every month and redeploy the VMs from them.
Use VM Manager OS patch management with patch deployments and compliance reporting.
Use a cron job on a bastion host that connects by SSH to every VM.
questions.correct_rationale: VM Manager's patch management schedules patch jobs across fleets and reports patch compliance.
questions.distractor_summary: Startup scripts only run on boot and don't report compliance, recreating machine images doesn't update running VMs, and a bastion cron job is fragile at this scale.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A regional managed instance group uses instance template `web-v1`. The team needs to change the machine type from `e2-medium` to `e2-standard-2` without downtime. What should the engineer do?
options: Edit `web-v1` in place and restart the MIG for the change.
Create `web-v2`, then start a rolling update using `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable`.
Stop each of the VMs and change its machine type one by one.
Delete the MIG and create a new one that uses the template `web-v2`.
questions.correct_rationale: Instance templates are immutable, so a new template is created and applied through a rolling update that replaces instances gradually.
questions.distractor_summary: Templates can't be edited, manually changing VMs in a MIG conflicts with the template, and deleting the MIG causes downtime.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An engineer created a GKE cluster named `prod-cluster` in region `us-east1` using the console. Running `kubectl get nodes` from Cloud Shell returns an error saying that no configuration was provided. What should the engineer run?
options: `kubectl config set-cluster prod-cluster` throughout the organization overall.
`gcloud auth application-default login` throughout the organization overall.
`gcloud container clusters get-credentials prod-cluster --region=us-east1`
`gcloud components install kubectl --cluster=prod-cluster` for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: `get-credentials` writes the cluster's endpoint and authentication details into the kubeconfig file so kubectl can connect.
questions.distractor_summary: Setting only the cluster name doesn't configure credentials, Application Default Credentials don't update kubeconfig, and installing kubectl doesn't take a cluster flag.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company's production GKE Standard cluster runs in a single zone. During a zonal outage, both the control plane and the workloads became unavailable. The company wants the control plane and nodes to survive the loss of a zone. What should the engineer create?
options: Use a regional cluster, which replicates the control plane and spreads nodes over zones.
Use a zonal cluster with a node pool in a second zone (multi-zonal) as a result across the setup.
Use two zonal clusters that are placed in the same zone for the application in the project.
Use a zonal cluster with a larger node count in the same zone in that case for the team at that point.
questions.correct_rationale: Regional clusters run multiple control plane replicas across zones and distribute nodes across zones, surviving a zone failure.
questions.distractor_summary: Multi-zonal clusters still have a single-zone control plane, and additional clusters or nodes in the same zone don't add zonal resilience.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Security requires that GKE nodes have only internal IP addresses. After creating a cluster with private nodes, the team finds that Pods can't pull public container images from Docker Hub. What should the engineer add?
options: Use external IP addresses on each of the nodes of the cluster.
Use Private Google Access on the node subnet of the cluster.
Use authorized networks on the control plane of the cluster.
Use a Cloud NAT gateway for the IP ranges of the node subnet.
questions.correct_rationale: Private nodes need Cloud NAT to reach internet destinations such as Docker Hub while keeping internal-only IPs.
questions.distractor_summary: External IPs violate policy, Private Google Access only reaches Google APIs such as Artifact Registry, and authorized networks control access to the control plane rather than node egress.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An engineer has a container image `us-docker.pkg.dev/acme/web/storefront:1.4` in Artifact Registry and wants to deploy three replicas to a GKE cluster and make it reachable from the internet on port 80 through a Google Cloud load balancer. What should the engineer do?
options: Run `gcloud run deploy` with the image and select the GKE cluster.
Create a three-replica Deployment, then a `LoadBalancer` Service that targets its Pods on port 80.
Create one Pod with the image and a Service of type `ClusterIP` for it.
Create a DaemonSet with the image and a Service of type `NodePort` for it.
questions.correct_rationale: A Deployment manages replicated Pods, and a `LoadBalancer` Service provisions an external load balancer for them.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud Run doesn't deploy to GKE this way, a single Pod with `ClusterIP` isn't replicated or externally reachable, and a DaemonSet runs one Pod per node rather than a set replica count.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A GKE cluster in project `apps-prod` fails to pull images from an Artifact Registry repository in project `shared-images`, with `ImagePullBackOff` errors indicating permission denied. Nodes use a custom service account `gke-nodes@apps-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com`. What should the engineer do?
options: Grant `roles/artifactregistry.reader` to the node service account on the repository or project.
Make the repository public so that the nodes can pull the images.
Grant `roles/owner` on `shared-images` to the node service account throughout the organization overall.
Copy the images into a Cloud Storage bucket in the `apps-prod` project throughout the organization.
questions.correct_rationale: Nodes pull images using their service account, which needs Artifact Registry Reader on the repository in the other project.
questions.distractor_summary: Making the repository public exposes images, Owner violates least privilege, and Cloud Storage isn't a container registry.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An application running in GKE Pods must read objects from a Cloud Storage bucket. The security team prohibits service account key files and wants each application to have its own identity rather than using the node's service account. What should the engineer configure?
options: Store a service account key in a Kubernetes Secret for the Pods throughout the organization for the team.
Grant the storage role to the node's Compute Engine default service account throughout the organization overall.
Enable Workload Identity Federation for GKE and grant a Storage role to the Kubernetes service account.
Make the bucket public-read so that the Pods can read the objects throughout the organization by default.
questions.correct_rationale: Workload Identity Federation for GKE lets Kubernetes service accounts authenticate to Google Cloud APIs without keys, and roles can be granted per application.
questions.distractor_summary: Key files violate policy, node service account permissions are shared by all Pods on the node, and public buckets expose data.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A GKE Standard cluster's default node pool uses `e2-standard-4` machines. A new in-memory analytics service needs nodes with 64 GB of memory, and only that service should run on them. What should the engineer do?
options: Change the machine type of the default node pool in place for the service across the setup.
Create a second cluster for the service that uses larger machines.
Increase the number of the nodes in the default node pool of the cluster.
Add a high-memory node pool with a taint, plus a toleration and selector on the Pods.
questions.correct_rationale: Adding a dedicated node pool with a taint and matching toleration and selector keeps the service on high-memory nodes and other workloads off them.
questions.distractor_summary: Machine types of existing node pools can't be changed in place, a second cluster adds overhead, and more small nodes don't provide a 64 GB node.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company operates 15 GKE clusters across several projects and regions. It wants to apply consistent Kubernetes configurations and security policies from a Git repository across all clusters and view them from a central place. What should the engineer use?
options: Use a separate CI pipeline for each cluster that runs `kubectl apply` overall.
Use GKE Enterprise fleet management with Config Sync and Policy Controller.
Use organization policies for the Kubernetes objects in the clusters.
Use Cloud Deployment Manager templates for the objects in each cluster overall.
questions.correct_rationale: GKE Enterprise fleets let you manage many clusters together, with Config Sync applying configuration from Git and Policy Controller enforcing policies.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-cluster pipelines drift and are hard to govern, organization policies don't manage Kubernetes objects, and Deployment Manager isn't designed for Kubernetes configuration.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploying Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions
questions.question: A developer has a Node.js application's source code in a local directory with no Dockerfile. The developer wants to deploy it to Cloud Run with a single command and without building the container image manually. What should the developer run?
options: `gcloud run deploy my-app --source .`, run from the source directory
`docker build` followed by `gcloud run deploy --image`, run from the directory
`gcloud app deploy`, run from the source directory of the application
`kubectl apply -f .`, run from the source directory of the application
questions.correct_rationale: `gcloud run deploy --source` uploads the source, builds a container with Cloud Build and buildpacks (or a Dockerfile if present), and deploys it.
questions.distractor_summary: A manual Docker build requires extra steps, `gcloud app deploy` targets App Engine, and kubectl targets Kubernetes.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploying Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions
questions.question: A company runs two Cloud Run services: a public `frontend` and an internal `orders` API. Only `frontend` should be able to call `orders`, and `orders` must reject unauthenticated requests from the internet. What should the engineer configure?
options: Make `orders` public and validate a shared secret header on every request.
Place both of the services in the same project, which allows the calls automatically.
Use `--no-allow-unauthenticated` and grant `roles/run.invoker` to `frontend`'s service account.
Use a Cloud Armor policy on the default URL of the `orders` service.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Run IAM requires callers to present identity tokens, and granting Invoker only to the frontend's service account restricts access.
questions.distractor_summary: Shared secrets are weaker, being in the same project doesn't grant invoke rights, and Cloud Armor can't be attached to a Cloud Run default URL.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploying Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions
questions.question: A data team wants a Cloud Run service to run automatically whenever a BigQuery job completes in its project, so it can post results to a dashboard. BigQuery doesn't publish these events directly to Pub/Sub. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use a Cloud Scheduler job that runs every minute to call the service.
Use a Cloud Storage notification on the BigQuery dataset to call the service overall.
Use a Cloud Monitoring alert that calls the service when a job completes by default.
Use an Eventarc trigger on the Cloud Audit Logs event for BigQuery job completion.
questions.correct_rationale: Eventarc can trigger on Cloud Audit Logs entries for Google Cloud service actions, delivering events such as BigQuery job completion to Cloud Run.
questions.distractor_summary: Scheduled polling adds delay and cost, Cloud Storage notifications don't apply to BigQuery, and Monitoring alerts aren't an event-routing mechanism.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploying Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions
questions.question: An order-processing Cloud Run service must receive messages published to a Pub/Sub topic. The service is deployed without unauthenticated access. How should the engineer connect Pub/Sub to the service?
options: Make the service public and use a pull subscription for the messages.
Create a push subscription to the service URL with auth, using an account with `roles/run.invoker`.
Grant Pub/Sub Publisher to the service account of the Cloud Run service.
Configure the service to poll the topic directly for the messages.
questions.correct_rationale: Authenticated push subscriptions send OIDC tokens for a service account that has Invoker on the private service.
questions.distractor_summary: Making it public weakens security, the publisher role lets the service publish rather than receive, and topics can't be polled directly without a subscription.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploying Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions
questions.question: A Cloud Run service runs a single-threaded image-processing library that uses 100% of a CPU per request. Under load, latency spikes because many requests share each instance. What should the engineer change?
options: Set the maximum concurrent requests per instance to 1 so each request gets its own instance.
Reduce the maximum number of instances that the service can use.
Increase the request timeout of the service to 60 minutes.
Change the ingress setting of the service to internal only.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Run allows up to 80 concurrent requests per instance by default, so CPU-bound single-threaded work should use a concurrency of 1 and scale out instead.
questions.distractor_summary: Fewer instances worsen contention, longer timeouts don't reduce latency, and ingress settings control who can reach the service.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploying Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions
questions.question: A Cloud Run service that loads a large ML model at startup sometimes takes 12 seconds to respond to the first request after periods of low traffic. The business wants to eliminate these cold starts during business hours, accepting some added cost. What should the engineer configure?
options: Increase the maximum instances to 100 so the model loads on more of them.
Set the concurrency of the service to 1 for each of the instances overall.
Set a minimum number of instances so that some of them remain warm.
Move the model into an environment variable of the service as needed.
questions.correct_rationale: Minimum instances keep containers initialized and ready to serve, avoiding cold starts at the cost of paying for idle instances.
questions.distractor_summary: Raising the maximum doesn't keep instances warm, lower concurrency can cause more cold starts, and environment variables can't hold large models.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploying Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions
questions.question: A Cloud Run service needs to connect to a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance. The team wants encrypted, IAM-authorized connections without managing SSL certificates or allowlisting IP addresses. What should the engineer do?
options: Give the instance a public IP and add `0.0.0.0/0` to the authorized networks in production.
Store the database password in the container image of the service.
Create a VPC Network Peering connection between Cloud Run and Cloud SQL for the application.
Configure the Cloud SQL connection and grant the service account `roles/cloudsql.client`.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Run's built-in Cloud SQL connection uses the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy mechanism to provide encrypted, IAM-authorized connections.
questions.distractor_summary: Opening the instance to the internet is insecure, embedding passwords in images is a security risk, and Cloud Run isn't a VPC that can be peered.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploying Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions
questions.question: A team wrote an event-driven Cloud Run function triggered by Pub/Sub messages. Some messages trigger processing that takes about 30 minutes, and the function times out. What should the engineer do?
options: Use a Cloud Run job for the long processing, since event-driven functions time out near 9 minutes.
Increase the timeout of the event-driven function to 60 minutes for the long job for the team at that point.
Increase the memory of the function to 32 GB for the long processing job.
Change the trigger from Pub/Sub to Cloud Storage for the long processing job.
questions.correct_rationale: Event-driven functions have a much lower maximum timeout than HTTP functions, so long tasks should run in Cloud Run jobs or another service designed for them.
questions.distractor_summary: The 60-minute limit applies to HTTP functions, more memory doesn't raise the timeout, and changing the trigger type doesn't change the event-driven limit.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company is deploying a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance for a production order system. The database must fail over automatically to another zone if its primary zone becomes unavailable, with no data loss for committed transactions. What should the engineer configure when creating the instance?
options: Use a single-zone instance with daily automated backups for the system for the application.
Use a high availability (regional) configuration, such as `--availability-type=REGIONAL`.
Use a cross-region read replica that an engineer promotes manually.
Use point-in-time recovery on a zonal instance for the system.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud SQL HA uses a standby in another zone with synchronous replication, and fails over automatically.
questions.distractor_summary: Backups and point-in-time recovery restore data but aren't automatic failover, and cross-region replicas are asynchronous and require manual promotion.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An engineer uploaded a SQL dump file to `gs://migration-dumps/orders.sql` and runs `gcloud sql import sql orders-db gs://migration-dumps/orders.sql`. The import fails with a permission error reading the file. What should the engineer do?
options: Make the bucket public so that the instance can read the dump throughout the organization in production.
Grant the engineer `roles/cloudsql.admin` on the project for the import throughout the organization overall.
Copy the file to Cloud Shell and import it from there for the instance throughout the organization overall.
Grant the instance's service account read access, such as `roles/storage.objectViewer`, on the bucket.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud SQL reads import files from Cloud Storage using the instance's service account, which needs read permissions on the bucket.
questions.distractor_summary: A public bucket exposes data, the engineer's own role isn't used to read the file, and imports must come from Cloud Storage rather than a local file.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A data analyst has 40 CSV files with header rows in `gs://sales-raw/2026/`. They need to load them into a new BigQuery table `analytics.sales` with minimal effort and no custom code, letting BigQuery infer the schema. What should the engineer run?
options: Run `bq load --autodetect --source_format=CSV analytics.sales "gs://sales-raw/2026/*.csv"` once.
Run `bq query "INSERT INTO analytics.sales SELECT * FROM gs://sales-raw/2026/*.csv"` once.
Run `gcloud storage cp "gs://sales-raw/2026/*.csv" bq://analytics.sales` as one step.
Run `gcloud dataflow jobs run csv-load --gcs-location=gs://sales-raw/2026/*.csv` once.
questions.correct_rationale: `bq load` with `--autodetect` loads CSV files from Cloud Storage with wildcards and infers the schema.
questions.distractor_summary: SQL can't read Cloud Storage paths directly without an external table, `gcloud storage cp` doesn't write to BigQuery, and a streaming pipeline is unnecessary for a batch load.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A retailer publishes clickstream events to a Pub/Sub topic. The analytics team wants events written continuously into a BigQuery table with minimal development effort and no servers to manage. What should the engineer deploy?
options: Use a Compute Engine VM that runs a custom subscriber script.
Use a Cloud Scheduler job that exports the Pub/Sub messages each hour for the application.
Use the Pub/Sub-to-BigQuery Dataflow template, or a BigQuery subscription on the topic.
Use a Cloud Storage bucket notification for the clickstream events.
questions.correct_rationale: Google-provided Dataflow templates and BigQuery subscriptions stream Pub/Sub messages into BigQuery without custom servers.
questions.distractor_summary: A VM requires management, Cloud Scheduler can't export messages this way, and Cloud Storage notifications aren't related to Pub/Sub ingestion.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An engineer needs to upload about 50 GB of files from a workstation with a fast internet connection to a Cloud Storage bucket as quickly as possible. What should the engineer use?
options: Use the console's upload button, one file at a time, for the files.
Run `gcloud storage cp -r ./data gs://bucket-name/`, which transfers in parallel.
Order a Transfer Appliance to move the files to the Cloud Storage bucket in that case.
Use Storage Transfer Service with an on-premises agent for the files for the team at that point.
questions.correct_rationale: `gcloud storage cp` uses parallelism by default and is well suited to uploading tens of gigabytes from a workstation.
questions.distractor_summary: The console is slow for large sets of files, Transfer Appliance is for hundreds of terabytes over limited bandwidth, and agent-based transfers are more setup than needed for a one-time 50 GB upload.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company must move 400 TB of archived video from its data center to Cloud Storage within six weeks. Its internet connection is 200 Mbps and is heavily used during business hours. What should the engineer recommend?
options: Use `gcloud storage cp` over the internet during the nights and weekends overall.
Use Storage Transfer Service with on-premises agents over the existing link overall.
Use an HA VPN with multiple tunnels to carry the data to the cloud by default.
Use a Transfer Appliance, which is shipped to the data center and sent back.
questions.correct_rationale: At 200 Mbps, 400 TB would take months even with full utilization, so an offline Transfer Appliance is the practical option.
questions.distractor_summary: Online tools and VPN are limited by the same link, and VPN adds encryption overhead rather than bandwidth.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company wants to copy new and changed files from an on-premises NFS file server to Cloud Storage every night, with managed scheduling, retries, and logging, and without writing scripts. What should the engineer use?
options: Use Storage Transfer Service with on-premises agents and a scheduled transfer job.
Use a cron job on the file server that runs `gcloud storage rsync` each night overall.
Use a Transfer Appliance each night to carry the new and changed files for the team.
Use Cloud Scheduler to call the Cloud Storage JSON API each night.
questions.correct_rationale: Storage Transfer Service supports on-premises file systems through agents and provides managed scheduling, incremental transfers, retries, and logging.
questions.distractor_summary: A cron script works but lacks managed features, Transfer Appliance is for bulk offline moves, and Cloud Scheduler alone doesn't perform file transfers.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A team is creating the first Firestore database for a new mobile app whose users are mostly in Europe. A teammate suggests picking any location now and changing it later if needed. What should the engineer advise?
options: The location can be changed at any time from the console for the database by default.
The location only affects billing and has no effect on latency for users.
Choose a European location now, since a database's location can't be changed later.
Firestore is global, so the database does not have a location.
questions.correct_rationale: A Firestore database's location is set at creation and can't be changed, and it affects latency and data residency.
questions.distractor_summary: Changing location later would require creating a new database and migrating data.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A startup wants to use Spanner for a new service that currently has a small dataset and low traffic, but expects growth. It wants to minimize initial costs while keeping the option to scale. How should the engineer size the instance?
options: Create a multi-region instance with 10 nodes to start with throughout the organization by default.
Create a regional instance with a small capacity, such as 100 processing units, and scale later.
Use Cloud SQL now and migrate to Spanner later with no changes needed throughout the organization.
Use Bigtable with a single node instead of Spanner for the service throughout the organization overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Spanner compute capacity can be provisioned in processing units, starting at 100, allowing small, low-cost instances that can scale without downtime.
questions.distractor_summary: Ten multi-region nodes overprovisions, migrating from Cloud SQL requires changes, and Bigtable isn't relational.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A subscriber to a Pub/Sub subscription repeatedly fails on a few malformed messages, which are redelivered indefinitely and slow down processing. The team wants these messages set aside after five failed delivery attempts for later inspection. What should the engineer configure?
options: Reduce the message retention duration of the subscription to 10 minutes throughout the organization overall.
Enable message ordering on the subscription for the malformed messages.
Delete the subscription and recreate it so that the messages are dropped throughout the organization.
Add a dead-letter topic with five delivery attempts, and grant the Pub/Sub service agent its roles.
questions.correct_rationale: Dead-letter topics capture messages that exceed the configured delivery attempts, and the Pub/Sub service agent needs publish and subscribe permissions to forward them.
questions.distractor_summary: Shorter retention drops messages, ordering doesn't fix malformed data, and recreating the subscription loses messages.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An engineer needs to create a VPC named `prod-net` with no automatically created subnets, and then a subnet `web-us` in `us-east1` with range `10.10.0.0/24`. Which commands should the engineer run?
options: `gcloud compute networks create prod-net --subnet-mode=custom`, then create `web-us` in `us-east1` with `10.10.0.0/24`.
`gcloud compute networks create prod-net --subnet-mode=auto`, then delete the extra subnets that it created.
`gcloud compute networks subnets create web-us --region=us-east1 --range=10.10.0.0/24`, with no network created first in the project.
`gcloud compute networks create prod-net --range=10.10.0.0/24`, then create `web-us` in `us-east1` by hand.
questions.correct_rationale: Custom subnet mode creates a VPC without subnets, and subnets are created per region with a specified range.
questions.distractor_summary: Auto mode creates subnets in every region, a subnet must belong to a network, and `--range` on network creation applies only to legacy networks.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Web servers tagged `web` in `prod-net` must accept HTTP and HTTPS from the internet. Other VMs in the network must not be exposed. What firewall rule should the engineer create?
options: Use an ingress rule that allows TCP 80 and 443 from `0.0.0.0/0` to all instances.
Use an egress rule that allows TCP 80 and 443 to `0.0.0.0/0` for the tag `web`.
Use an ingress rule that allows TCP 80 and 443 from `0.0.0.0/0` with target tag `web`.
Use an ingress rule that allows all protocols from `0.0.0.0/0` with target tag `web` overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Target tags limit the rule to tagged VMs, and specifying ports 80 and 443 follows least privilege.
questions.distractor_summary: Applying to all instances exposes other VMs, egress rules don't allow inbound traffic, and allowing all protocols is overly permissive.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A security team wants to prevent all VMs in a VPC from sending traffic to a known malicious network `203.0.113.0/24`, while other egress remains allowed. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use an ingress deny rule from `203.0.113.0/24` on the VPC network.
Use a route for `203.0.113.0/24` with the default internet gateway as next hop.
Remove the implied allow egress rule so that all egress traffic is blocked.
Use an egress deny rule to `203.0.113.0/24` on all instances, with a priority above egress allows.
questions.correct_rationale: An egress deny rule blocks outbound traffic to the destination, and it must have higher precedence (a lower priority number) than any matching allow rules.
questions.distractor_summary: Ingress rules don't block outbound traffic, a route to the internet gateway permits the traffic, and implied rules can't be removed.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A team's firewall rules target VMs using network tags, but any developer who can edit instances can add tags and gain access through the rules. The team wants firewall targeting tied to VM identity. What should the engineer use?
options: Use labels as the targets of the firewall rules for the VMs throughout the organization.
Use target service accounts in the rules, with the VMs running as dedicated accounts.
Use a separate VPC for every one of the VMs of the team throughout the organization overall.
Use firewall rules with source tags only, without any target throughout the organization.
questions.correct_rationale: Firewall rules can target VMs by service account, and changing a VM's service account requires more privileged permissions than editing tags.
questions.distractor_summary: Labels can't be firewall targets, per-VM VPCs are impractical, and source tags still rely on editable tags.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A network team enabled `net-host` as a Shared VPC host project. A developer in the `app-dev` project can't select any `net-host` subnet when creating a VM. What must the Shared VPC Admin do?
options: Attach `app-dev` as a service project, and grant `roles/compute.networkUser` on the needed subnets.
Create VPC Network Peering between `app-dev` and `net-host` for the developer to use.
Grant the developer the Owner role on the `net-host` host project.
Move the creation of the VM into the `net-host` project for the developer.
questions.correct_rationale: Service projects must be attached to the host project, and users need Network User on the shared subnets to use them.
questions.distractor_summary: Peering isn't how Shared VPC works, Owner violates least privilege, and creating VMs in the host project defeats the service project model.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An engineer created a VPC Network Peering connection from `vpc-a` to `vpc-b` in another project. The peering shows a state of `INACTIVE`, and no routes are exchanged. What is the most likely reason?
options: The VPCs are in different regions, so the peering stays inactive for them.
Peering requires Cloud VPN between the two VPCs before it becomes active.
The administrator of `vpc-b` has not yet created the matching peering back to `vpc-a`.
Firewall rules are blocking the peering between the two of the VPCs.
questions.correct_rationale: Peering becomes active only after both networks create peering connections to each other.
questions.distractor_summary: VPCs are global, so regions don't matter; peering doesn't need VPN; and firewall rules affect traffic after peering, not its state.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An engineer is building an HA VPN connection to an on-premises firewall with two public IP addresses. Which set of Google Cloud resources must be created?
options: Use a Classic VPN gateway with one tunnel and a static route to the firewall.
Use a Cloud NAT gateway and two external IP addresses for the on-premises firewall.
Use a VPC peering connection to the on-premises network of the firewall.
Use an HA VPN gateway, a peer gateway with two interfaces, a Cloud Router, two tunnels and BGP.
questions.correct_rationale: HA VPN requires an HA VPN gateway, a peer gateway resource describing the on-premises interfaces, a Cloud Router, tunnels, and BGP sessions.
questions.distractor_summary: Classic VPN isn't HA VPN, Cloud NAT is for outbound internet access, and peering can't connect to on-premises networks.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An engineer created an external Application Load Balancer for a managed instance group. The backends show as unhealthy, although the application works when tested directly from inside the VPC. Which firewall rule should the engineer add?
options: Allow ingress from `0.0.0.0/0` on all ports to the backend VMs for the application.
Allow ingress from `35.191.0.0/16` and `130.211.0.0/22` on the health check port.
Allow egress to `35.191.0.0/16` from the backend VMs on the health check port overall.
Allow ingress from `35.235.240.0/20` on port 22 to the backend VMs in every region.
questions.correct_rationale: Google Cloud health checks originate from `35.191.0.0/16` and `130.211.0.0/22`, so backends must allow ingress from those ranges on the health check port.
questions.distractor_summary: Opening all ports is excessive, egress is already allowed and doesn't admit probes, and `35.235.240.0/20` is used by IAP TCP forwarding.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company has 25 VPCs in projects under the `Production` folder. Security wants a single set of firewall rules, such as blocking inbound RDP from the internet, applied to all of them and future VPCs in that folder. What should the engineer create?
options: Use a hierarchical firewall policy associated with the `Production` folder.
Use a script to put the same VPC firewall rules in all 25 VPCs in production.
Use an organization policy constraint for the firewall ports of the VPCs overall.
Use a Cloud Armor policy on every VM in the 25 VPCs.
questions.correct_rationale: Hierarchical firewall policies apply to every VPC under the folder or organization they're associated with, including future ones.
questions.distractor_summary: Scripted per-VPC rules drift and don't cover new VPCs automatically, there's no organization policy for firewall ports, and Cloud Armor attaches to load balancers rather than VMs.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.6 Implementing resources via infrastructure as code
questions.question: A team of five engineers uses Terraform to manage Google Cloud infrastructure. They keep state files on their laptops, and recent concurrent runs corrupted infrastructure. What should the engineer configure?
options: Commit the state file to the Git repository after each run.
Store the state file in a shared Filestore instance for the engineers for the team.
Use a Cloud Storage backend with object versioning, which supports state locking.
Run Terraform only from one engineer's laptop for the whole team.
questions.correct_rationale: The Cloud Storage backend stores shared remote state with locking to prevent concurrent writes, and versioning allows recovery.
questions.distractor_summary: Committing state to Git risks secrets and conflicts, a file share doesn't provide Terraform locking semantics, and a single laptop is a bottleneck and single point of failure.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.6 Implementing resources via infrastructure as code
questions.question: An engineer suspects that someone manually changed firewall rules in the console that are managed by Terraform. Before applying new changes, the engineer wants to see exactly what Terraform would modify, including any drift. What should the engineer run?
options: `terraform apply -auto-approve`, which changes the resources to match the code at that point.
`terraform init -upgrade`, which upgrades the providers and the modules in the project as a result.
`terraform destroy`, which removes all of the resources in the state.
`terraform plan`, which shows the differences between the state and the real resources.
questions.correct_rationale: `terraform plan` refreshes the actual state and shows proposed changes, revealing drift without modifying anything.
questions.distractor_summary: Applying with auto-approve makes changes without review, `init` configures providers and backends, and `destroy` removes resources.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.6 Implementing resources via infrastructure as code
questions.question: A platform team manages all workloads through Kubernetes manifests and GitOps. It wants to create and manage Google Cloud resources such as Cloud Storage buckets, Pub/Sub topics, and Cloud SQL instances using Kubernetes YAML in the same workflow. What should the engineer use?
options: Use Helm charts that call gcloud to create the Google Cloud resources across the subscriptions.
Use Config Connector, which represents Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes custom resources.
Use Cloud Deployment Manager to create the Google Cloud resources throughout the organization overall.
Use startup scripts on the GKE nodes to create the Google Cloud resources across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: Config Connector lets you declare Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes objects and reconciles them, fitting a GitOps workflow.
questions.distractor_summary: Helm packages Kubernetes manifests but doesn't manage cloud resources on its own, Deployment Manager is separate from Kubernetes, and node startup scripts aren't declarative infrastructure management.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.6 Implementing resources via infrastructure as code
questions.question: A team deploys the same Kubernetes application, consisting of a Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, and HorizontalPodAutoscaler, to development, staging, and production clusters with different replica counts and image tags. It wants a packaged, versioned template with per-environment values. What should the engineer use?
options: Use Helm charts with separate values files for each of the environments.
Use Terraform with a Cloud Storage backend only for the application overall.
Copy and edit the YAML files for each one of the environments for the team.
Use Cloud Run services in place of the Kubernetes application.
questions.correct_rationale: Helm packages Kubernetes manifests as versioned charts, with values files for environment-specific configuration.
questions.distractor_summary: Terraform alone isn't a Kubernetes packaging tool, copying YAML leads to drift, and Cloud Run isn't Kubernetes.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.6 Implementing resources via infrastructure as code
questions.question: A company is building its Google Cloud landing zone and wants to use Google-maintained, opinionated Terraform modules and blueprints for projects, networking, and IAM that follow best practices, rather than writing everything from scratch. What should the engineer use?
options: Use Cloud Shell Editor templates for the landing zone of the company.
Use `gcloud` scripts that are written by the team for the landing zone.
Use Cloud Foundation Toolkit Terraform modules and blueprints for the landing zone.
Use Deployment Manager Jinja examples for the landing zone of the company by default.
questions.correct_rationale: The Cloud Foundation Toolkit provides Google-maintained Terraform modules and blueprints for common foundations such as projects, networks, and IAM. The other options require writing and maintaining most of the logic yourself, and Deployment Manager isn't the recommended IaC path.

questions.domain: 3. Deploying and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.subdomain: 3.6 Implementing resources via infrastructure as code
questions.question: A company wants to run Terraform deployments of Google Cloud resources from a managed Google Cloud service, with state stored and managed for it, IAM-controlled access, and no self-hosted CI runners. What should the engineer use?
options: Run Terraform on a Compute Engine VM with a cron job for the deployments.
Use Cloud Deployment Manager as the managed service for the deployments.
Use Config Connector as the managed service for the Terraform deployments.
Use Infrastructure Manager, the managed service for Terraform deployments.
questions.correct_rationale: Infrastructure Manager is a managed service that runs Terraform configurations on Google Cloud and manages state.
questions.distractor_summary: A VM with cron is self-managed, Deployment Manager doesn't run Terraform, and Config Connector uses Kubernetes resources rather than Terraform configurations.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company runs 40 Compute Engine VMs whose persistent disks must be backed up every night at 2:00 AM, with backups kept for 14 days and older ones deleted automatically. The team doesn't want to maintain scripts. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use a snapshot schedule policy with a daily start time and 14-day retention, on the disks.
Use a cron job on each VM that runs `gcloud compute disks snapshot` for the disks as needed.
Use a machine image that is created by hand each night for each of the VMs.
Use Object Lifecycle Management on a bucket where the disks are copied each night as needed.
questions.correct_rationale: Snapshot schedules automatically create and delete snapshots on a set schedule and retention period when attached to disks.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-VM cron jobs and manual machine images require maintenance, and persistent disks aren't copied into Cloud Storage buckets for lifecycle management.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A team needs to create an exact copy of a configured VM, including its three attached disks, machine type, metadata, labels, and network settings, to build an identical test environment. What should the engineer create?
options: Create a custom image from the boot disk of the configured VM.
Create a snapshot of the boot disk of the configured VM only.
Create a machine image of the VM, which keeps the attached disks and settings.
Create an instance template from scratch that matches the configured VM overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Machine images capture a VM's configuration, metadata, permissions, and data from all attached disks, making them ideal for cloning full VMs.
questions.distractor_summary: Custom images and snapshots capture single disks, and a new instance template wouldn't include disk data.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company builds a hardened OS image monthly and wants new VMs and instance templates to always use the latest approved image, while being able to mark older images as obsolete. What should the engineer do?
options: Store the image in Cloud Storage and download it each time that a VM boots up.
Create each image in an image family, use the family in templates, and deprecate old ones.
Use a machine image for each of the new VMs that the team creates.
Snapshot the golden VM monthly and create the disks from the latest snapshot.
questions.correct_rationale: Image families always resolve to the newest non-deprecated image, and deprecating images signals they should no longer be used.
questions.distractor_summary: Downloading images at boot isn't how VMs are created, machine images are for full VM copies, and snapshots don't provide family-based versioning.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An auditor asks for a list of all Compute Engine VMs across 60 projects in the organization that have the label `env=prod`, along with their zones and status. What is the most efficient way to produce it?
options: Log in to each project in the console and export its list of VMs across the subscriptions.
Run `gcloud compute instances list` in each project and merge the results in every region.
Check the billing export for the VM names across the projects throughout the organization.
Use Cloud Asset Inventory at the organization scope, filtering by asset type and label.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Asset Inventory searches resources across the whole organization with filters for type and labels.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-project console or CLI queries are slow and error-prone, and billing exports don't reliably list current VM status or zone.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An administrator needs to SSH into a VM that has no external IP address. The company has no VPN or bastion host and wants access controlled by IAM. A firewall rule allows TCP 22 from `35.235.240.0/20`. What should the administrator run?
options: `gcloud compute ssh vm-name --zone=us-central1-a --tunnel-through-iap`
`gcloud compute ssh vm-name --zone=us-central1-a --internal-ip`
`ssh user@<external-ip>` from the workstation of the administrator overall.
`gcloud compute connect-to-serial-port vm-name` for all of the administration
questions.correct_rationale: IAP TCP forwarding tunnels SSH to VMs without external IPs, controlled by IAM and the IAP firewall range.
questions.distractor_summary: Connecting to the internal IP requires existing network connectivity to the VPC, there's no external IP to use, and the serial console is meant for troubleshooting rather than routine administration.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A VM running a reporting application needs more memory, so the engineer tries to change its machine type from `n2-standard-4` to `n2-highmem-4` while it's running, and the operation fails. What must the engineer do?
options: Create a snapshot first, since machine types can only change from snapshots.
Add a second boot disk to the VM before changing the machine type.
Stop the VM, change the machine type, and start the VM again.
Delete the VM and recreate it with the same name and a new type.
questions.correct_rationale: A VM's machine type can be changed only while it's stopped, after which it can be restarted with the new configuration.
questions.distractor_summary: Snapshots aren't required, disks don't affect machine type, and recreating the VM is unnecessary.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company's application runs on a VM in `us-east1`. For a disaster recovery drill, the team must restore the VM's data disk in `us-west1` from last night's snapshot. What should the engineer do?
options: Export the regional snapshot to Cloud Storage and import it in `us-west1` for the team.
Move the original VM to `us-west1` with `gcloud compute instances move` in every region.
Create a machine image in `us-east1` and copy it with Storage Transfer Service overall.
Create a new disk in a `us-west1` zone from the snapshot and attach it to a VM there.
questions.correct_rationale: Snapshots are stored in multi-regional or regional Cloud Storage locations and can be used to create disks in other regions.
questions.distractor_summary: Exporting isn't required, moving the production VM isn't a restore drill, and Storage Transfer Service doesn't copy machine images.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A Deployment's Pods are in `CrashLoopBackOff`. `kubectl get pods` shows repeated restarts, and the current container logs are empty because the container just restarted. How should the engineer see why the previous container crashed?
options: Run `kubectl delete pod` and watch the Pod restart for the cause.
Run `kubectl logs <pod-name> --previous` and `kubectl describe pod` for events and exit codes.
Check the VPC Flow Logs for the Pods that keep crashing in the cluster across the subscriptions.
Run `gcloud container clusters describe` for the cluster that hosts the Pods for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: `kubectl logs --previous` shows logs from the prior crashed container, and `describe` shows events such as exit codes and OOM kills.
questions.distractor_summary: Deleting the Pod loses context, flow logs show network flows, and cluster descriptions don't show Pod-level crash reasons.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A web Deployment in GKE has three replicas. During daily traffic peaks, Pod CPU utilization exceeds 90% and latency increases. The team wants the number of Pods to increase automatically when average CPU exceeds 70%, up to 20 replicas. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use a HorizontalPodAutoscaler at 70% CPU with `minReplicas: 3` and `maxReplicas: 20`.
Use a VerticalPodAutoscaler in `Auto` mode for the Deployment of the web tier.
Use the cluster autoscaler only, without any Pod autoscaler for the Deployment at that point.
Use a larger node machine type for the node pool that runs the Deployment.
questions.correct_rationale: The HPA adjusts replica counts based on metrics such as CPU utilization relative to requests.
questions.distractor_summary: VPA changes Pod resource requests rather than count, cluster autoscaler adds nodes but doesn't add Pods, and larger nodes don't add replicas.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Developers set CPU and memory requests for their Pods by guesswork. Some Pods are OOM-killed, and others reserve far more than they use, wasting node capacity. The team wants GKE to recommend or automatically adjust requests based on actual usage. What should the engineer enable?
options: Use a HorizontalPodAutoscaler to set the Pod requests for the Deployments in Azure.
Use node auto-upgrade to set the Pod requests for the Deployments.
Use Pod disruption budgets to set the Pod requests for the Deployments.
Use a VerticalPodAutoscaler for the Deployments to recommend or set the requests.
questions.correct_rationale: VPA analyzes usage and recommends or automatically sets CPU and memory requests.
questions.distractor_summary: HPA scales replica count, auto-upgrade manages node versions, and disruption budgets limit voluntary disruptions.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: After a traffic surge, several Pods in a GKE Standard cluster remain in `Pending` with events saying there are insufficient CPU resources on nodes. The node pool has a fixed size of 3. What should the engineer do so capacity grows automatically in the future?
options: Enable the VerticalPodAutoscaler on the Deployment of the Pending Pods in every region.
Increase the replica count of the Deployment of the Pending Pods across the subscriptions.
Enable the cluster autoscaler on the node pool with minimum and maximum node counts.
Delete the Pending Pods and let the Deployment create them again.
questions.correct_rationale: The cluster autoscaler adds nodes when Pods can't be scheduled due to insufficient resources and removes underused nodes.
questions.distractor_summary: VPA doesn't add nodes, more replicas create more pending Pods, and deleting them doesn't add capacity.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A team is deploying a three-node distributed database on GKE. Each replica needs a stable network identity (for example, `db-0`, `db-1`, `db-2`) and its own persistent volume that stays with it when Pods are rescheduled. Which Kubernetes resource should the engineer use?
options: Use a Deployment with one shared PersistentVolumeClaim for the replicas overall.
Use a StatefulSet with `volumeClaimTemplates` for the three database replicas.
Use a DaemonSet so that every node runs one replica of the database for the team.
Use a Job that runs the three replicas of the database to completion by default.
questions.correct_rationale: StatefulSets give each Pod a stable name and ordinal and create a dedicated persistent volume per replica through volume claim templates.
questions.distractor_summary: Deployments treat Pods as interchangeable, DaemonSets run one Pod per node, and Jobs run to completion.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A retailer's GKE cluster has auto-upgrades enabled. The company wants upgrades to happen only on weekend nights and to be blocked entirely during the two-week holiday shopping season. What should the engineer configure?
options: Disable the auto-upgrade permanently on the cluster of the retailer in that case for the team.
Pin the cluster to one specific GKE version forever and skip upgrades as a result across the setup.
Set a Pod disruption budget of zero for the Deployments in the cluster in the project.
Set a weekend-night maintenance window and an exclusion covering the holiday period.
questions.correct_rationale: Maintenance windows control when automatic maintenance can occur, and exclusions block it during specified periods.
questions.distractor_summary: Disabling upgrades or pinning versions leaves clusters unpatched and unsupported, and a zero disruption budget can block node drains without scheduling upgrades.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A new image version was rolled out to a Deployment with `kubectl set image`, and error rates immediately increased. The team needs to return to the previous version as quickly as possible. What should the engineer run?
options: Run `kubectl delete deployment web` and recreate it from the old manifest overall.
Run `kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=0` to stop the bad rollout overall.
Run `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web` to return to the previous revision.
Run `gcloud container clusters upgrade --rollback` for the cluster.
questions.correct_rationale: `kubectl rollout undo` reverts a Deployment to its previous revision using its rollout history.
questions.distractor_summary: Deleting or scaling to zero causes an outage, and cluster upgrade rollbacks don't apply to application rollouts.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A team wants to deploy version 2 of a Cloud Run service and test it through a dedicated URL before any production traffic reaches it. What should the engineer do?
options: Deploy version 2 to a separate project for testing before the release across the subscriptions.
Deploy with `gcloud run deploy --no-traffic --tag=v2`, then test the tagged revision URL.
Deploy normally and roll back if the tests fail on the new revision.
Set the minimum instances to 0 on version 1 while version 2 is tested.
questions.correct_rationale: Deploying with `--no-traffic` creates a revision without routing production traffic, and a tag provides a dedicated URL for testing.
questions.distractor_summary: A separate project duplicates configuration, a normal deploy exposes users immediately, and minimum instances don't control routing.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: After testing, the team wants to send 10% of production traffic to Cloud Run revision `checkout-00012` and keep 90% on the current revision, then increase gradually. What should the engineer run?
options: Run `gcloud run services update-traffic checkout --to-revisions=checkout-00012=10` to split traffic.
Run `gcloud run deploy checkout --traffic=10` to send a tenth of the traffic.
Run `gcloud run services update checkout --max-instances=10` to cap the instances.
Create a second service and a load balancer with weighted DNS records.
questions.correct_rationale: `update-traffic` with `--to-revisions` splits traffic by percentage between revisions of a service.
questions.distractor_summary: The other flags don't exist or control scaling, and separate services with DNS weighting are unnecessarily complex.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Minutes after a new Cloud Run revision received 100% of traffic, customers report errors. The previous revision is still available. What's the fastest way to restore service?
options: Rebuild the previous container image and redeploy it as a new revision in Azure.
Delete the service and recreate it from the previous configuration for the team.
Increase the memory limit of the new revision and deploy it again.
Route 100% of the traffic back to the previous revision with `update-traffic`.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Run keeps previous revisions, so traffic can be routed back immediately without rebuilding.
questions.distractor_summary: Rebuilding takes longer, deleting causes an outage, and changing memory may not fix the defect.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A Cloud Run service connects to a Cloud SQL instance that supports at most 200 connections. During a traffic spike, Cloud Run scaled out to hundreds of instances and exhausted database connections, causing errors. What should the engineer configure?
options: Set the minimum instances to 100 so that connections are spread out.
Increase the request timeout of the service so that connections are reused for the team.
Set a maximum number of instances so total connections stay within the database limit.
Enable CPU boost at startup so that connections are opened faster.
questions.correct_rationale: Maximum instances cap scale-out, which protects downstream systems with limited connection capacity.
questions.distractor_summary: More minimum instances increase connections, longer timeouts don't limit connections, and CPU boost only speeds up startup.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A Cloud Run service returns an HTTP response quickly but then continues processing data in background threads for several seconds. The background work is often throttled or doesn't complete. What should the engineer configure?
options: Set the concurrency of the service to 1 for each of the instances.
Set CPU to always allocated (instance-based billing) so instances get CPU outside of requests.
Increase the maximum number of instances that the service can use.
Change the ingress of the service to internal only for the callers.
questions.correct_rationale: With request-based billing, CPU is only allocated while handling requests, so background work after the response is throttled; always-allocated CPU fixes this.
questions.distractor_summary: Concurrency, maximum instances, and ingress don't affect CPU availability outside requests.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A bucket with Object Versioning enabled is growing quickly because every overwrite keeps the old version forever. The team wants to keep noncurrent versions for 30 days and then delete them automatically. What should the engineer configure?
options: Add a lifecycle rule that deletes noncurrent objects older than 30 days (`daysSinceNoncurrentTime: 30`).
Disable Object Versioning on the bucket that is growing quickly throughout the organization in production.
Set a retention policy of 30 days on the bucket that is growing quickly throughout the organization overall.
Use a cron job that lists and deletes the old versions in the bucket throughout the organization in Azure.
questions.correct_rationale: Lifecycle rules can target noncurrent versions based on how long they've been noncurrent, deleting them automatically.
questions.distractor_summary: Disabling versioning removes protection, a retention policy prevents deletion rather than causing it, and a cron job adds maintenance.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company needs to let an external customer download a single private report from Cloud Storage for 24 hours, without creating a Google account for them or making the object public. What should the engineer do?
options: Grant `allUsers` the Reader role on the object for the customer.
Grant the customer's email the `roles/storage.objectViewer` role on the whole bucket.
Copy the report to a public bucket for the customer to download.
Generate a signed URL for the object with a 24-hour expiration.
questions.correct_rationale: Signed URLs give time-limited access to a specific object to anyone who has the URL, without requiring a Google account.
questions.distractor_summary: Public access exposes the object to everyone, IAM requires a Google identity, and a public bucket removes access control.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A brokerage firm must keep trade confirmation records in Cloud Storage for seven years in a write-once, read-many (WORM) manner. Nobody, including administrators, may delete or overwrite them before seven years. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use Object Versioning with a lifecycle rule on the bucket of records for the team.
Use uniform bucket-level access and IAM deny policies on the bucket.
Set a seven-year retention policy on the bucket, then lock it with Bucket Lock.
Use the Archive storage class for the bucket of the trade records.
questions.correct_rationale: A locked retention policy prevents deletion or modification of objects until their retention period ends, and the lock is irreversible, satisfying WORM requirements.
questions.distractor_summary: Versioning and IAM can be changed by administrators, and storage class doesn't prevent deletion.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An analyst wants to know how much a large BigQuery query will cost under on-demand pricing before running it. What should the engineer recommend?
options: Run the query with `LIMIT 10` to reduce the cost of the query throughout the organization overall.
Run the query as a dry run, such as `bq query --dry_run`, to see the bytes it will process.
Check Cloud Monitoring after the query has been run to see the cost across the subscriptions.
Export the table to Cloud Storage first to find the size of the query across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: A dry run estimates the bytes processed without running the query, which determines on-demand cost. `LIMIT` usually doesn't reduce bytes scanned, checking after running doesn't prevent cost, and exporting doesn't estimate query cost.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: At 14:32, a developer accidentally ran a `DELETE` without a `WHERE` clause on a production Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL table. Automated backups and point-in-time recovery are enabled. The team wants to recover the data as it was at 14:31 without overwriting the current instance. What should the engineer do?
options: Use point-in-time recovery to clone the instance to 14:31, then copy the data back.
Restore last night's automated backup onto the production instance for the application.
Promote a read replica of the production instance to a new primary for the application.
Export the table from the current instance and import it again.
questions.correct_rationale: Point-in-time recovery creates a new instance at a specific timestamp, allowing data recovery without affecting production.
questions.distractor_summary: Restoring last night's backup loses today's changes and overwrites production, read replicas already applied the delete, and exporting captures the deleted state.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company uses Firestore for a customer-facing app and must be able to restore data from any day in the past week after an application bug corrupts records. What should the engineer set up?
options: Use Object Versioning on a Cloud Storage bucket for the Firestore data.
Use Cloud SQL automated backups for the Firestore data of the app.
Use a Memorystore replica of the Firestore database for the app.
Use Firestore scheduled backups with seven-day retention, or scheduled managed exports.
questions.correct_rationale: Firestore supports scheduled backups with configurable retention and managed exports to Cloud Storage for restoring data.
questions.distractor_summary: Bucket versioning and Cloud SQL backups don't apply to Firestore, and Memorystore isn't a Firestore backup.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An engineer needs to check, from the command line, whether a Dataflow pipeline launched overnight is still running and whether a BigQuery load job succeeded. Which commands should the engineer use?
options: Run `gcloud compute instances list` and `gcloud logging read` for the job as a result across the setup.
Run `kubectl get jobs` against the cluster for both the pipeline and the table in the project.
Run `gcloud dataflow jobs list --status=active`, then `bq show -j <job_id>` for the load.
Run `gcloud run jobs list` and `bq ls` to see the status of the pipeline.
questions.correct_rationale: `gcloud dataflow jobs` shows pipeline status, and `bq show -j` displays a BigQuery job's state and errors.
questions.distractor_summary: Compute Engine and kubectl commands don't track these services, and Cloud Run jobs and `bq ls` don't show these job statuses.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An engineer needs to run a few ad hoc SQL queries against a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance from Cloud Shell to verify data after a migration, without configuring IP allowlists manually. What should the engineer do?
options: Open port 3306 to `0.0.0.0/0` on the instance and connect directly from the laptop as needed.
Run `gcloud sql connect <instance> --user=<user>` from Cloud Shell to open a MySQL session.
Export the whole database to CSV files and inspect the results locally.
Use `bq query` against the instance after creating a federated connection for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: `gcloud sql connect` handles temporary access for the client and starts a database session, which is convenient for ad hoc queries.
questions.distractor_summary: Opening the instance to the internet is insecure, exporting is slow, and `bq query` targets BigQuery (federated queries require separate setup).

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A VM with an ephemeral external IP address hosts an API that partners have allowlisted by IP. The team must stop and restart the VM for maintenance and doesn't want the IP to change. What should the engineer do before stopping the VM?
options: Promote the VM's current ephemeral external IP to a static external IP address.
Take a snapshot of the VM before maintenance and restore it on a new VM.
Reserve a new static IP and send it to the partners after the maintenance overall.
Add the current IP to a firewall rule that permits the partners' traffic.
questions.correct_rationale: An in-use ephemeral IP can be promoted to a static address, keeping the same IP across stops and starts.
questions.distractor_summary: Snapshots don't preserve IPs, a new IP requires partners to update allowlists, and firewall rules don't reserve addresses.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Application servers connect to a self-managed database VM by its internal IP address. When the database VM was recreated, it received a different internal IP and applications broke. What should the engineer configure?
options: Assign an external IP to the database VM and connect through that address for the team.
Use an ephemeral internal IP and extend the DHCP lease on the VM across the subscriptions.
Place the database VM behind Cloud NAT so the address is stable across the subscriptions.
Reserve a static internal IP address in the subnet and assign it to the database VM.
questions.correct_rationale: Static internal IP addresses remain reserved in the subnet and can be reassigned to a recreated VM. External IPs expose the database, ephemeral internal IPs don't persist across recreation, and Cloud NAT handles outbound internet traffic.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company with an existing custom mode VPC `prod-net` is expanding to Asia and needs VMs in `asia-northeast1`. The VPC currently has subnets only in the US and Europe. What should the engineer do?
options: Create a new VPC for Asia and peer it with `prod-net` to connect both in every region.
Expand an existing US subnet so that it also covers the Asia region.
Create a new subnet in `asia-northeast1` in `prod-net` with a non-overlapping range.
Switch `prod-net` to auto mode so that it adds a subnet in each region in every region.
questions.correct_rationale: VPCs are global, so adding a subnet in the new region extends the same network.
questions.distractor_summary: A separate peered VPC adds complexity, subnets are regional and can't span regions, and auto mode creates subnets in every region with fixed ranges.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company hosts the public zone `example.com` in Cloud DNS. It needs to add an A record so that `app.example.com` points to a load balancer at `34.120.10.5` with a TTL of 300 seconds. What should the engineer run?
options: Run `gcloud compute addresses create app --address=34.120.10.5` to publish the address.
Run `gcloud dns record-sets create app.example.com. --zone=example-zone --type=A --rrdatas=34.120.10.5`
Run `gcloud dns managed-zones create app.example.com --dns-name=34.120.10.5` for the name.
Edit `/etc/hosts` on each client to map `app.example.com` to the new address.
questions.correct_rationale: `gcloud dns record-sets create` adds a record with the specified type, TTL, and data to a managed zone.
questions.distractor_summary: Reserving an address doesn't create DNS records, creating a managed zone doesn't add the A record, and editing hosts files isn't DNS management.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: VMs without external IP addresses in `us-central1` need outbound internet access to download software updates, but must not be reachable from the internet. What should the engineer create?
options: A Cloud Router in `us-central1` and a Cloud NAT gateway for the subnets.
External IP addresses on all of the VMs, plus an ingress deny firewall rule.
Private Google Access turned on for the subnets that hold the VMs.
An internal passthrough load balancer in front of the VMs in the region.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud NAT, configured on a Cloud Router, provides outbound internet access without allowing unsolicited inbound connections.
questions.distractor_summary: External IPs expose the VMs, Private Google Access only covers Google APIs, and an internal load balancer doesn't provide internet egress.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A company wants the on-call team to be notified by SMS and email whenever its public website at `https://www.example.com` is unreachable from multiple locations. What should the engineer configure?
options: A log-based metric on the load balancer logs, with an alert on its count by default.
VPC Flow Logs for the web servers, with a sink to Pub/Sub for the team in production.
A dashboard that shows CPU utilization for the web servers over time in every region.
An uptime check on the URL, with an alert policy that uses SMS and email channels.
questions.correct_rationale: Uptime checks probe endpoints from multiple global locations, and alerting policies notify channels such as SMS and email when checks fail.
questions.distractor_summary: Logs and flow logs don't actively probe availability, and dashboards don't send notifications.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An application team wants to track the number of completed checkouts per minute as a metric in Cloud Monitoring and alert when it drops. This value isn't available as a built-in metric. What should the engineer recommend?
options: Enable VPC Flow Logs on the subnet and count the connections to the app.
Use the default CPU utilization metric as a proxy for completed checkouts for the application.
Write a custom metric from the app (OpenTelemetry or the Monitoring API) and alert on it.
Enable Data Access audit logs and count the matching log entries per minute in every region.
questions.correct_rationale: Custom metrics let applications publish business-specific values to Cloud Monitoring for dashboards and alerts.
questions.distractor_summary: Flow logs and audit logs don't count checkouts, and CPU utilization is a poor proxy for business activity.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An application writes log entries containing `PAYMENT_GATEWAY_TIMEOUT` when a third-party call fails. The team wants an alert when more than 20 such entries occur within five minutes. The application can't be modified. What should the engineer create?
options: An uptime check on the payment gateway endpoint, with an alert on failures.
A counter log-based metric on the log text, with an alert at 20 in five minutes.
A log sink to BigQuery, with a scheduled query that checks the count of entries overall.
A custom metric written by the application, with an alert on its value.
questions.correct_rationale: Log-based metrics convert matching log entries into metrics that can drive alerting policies, without application changes.
questions.distractor_summary: Uptime checks don't read logs, BigQuery sinks are for analysis rather than alerting, and custom metrics require code changes.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A security team needs all audit logs from every project in the organization copied to a central BigQuery dataset for long-term analysis, and separately streamed to an on-premises SIEM. What should the engineer configure?
options: Organization-level aggregated sinks with `--include-children`: one to BigQuery and one to Pub/Sub.
A log sink in each project that routes the audit logs to Cloud Storage buckets across the subscriptions.
Cloud Monitoring dashboards that show the audit log volume of every project across the subscriptions.
Enable Data Access logs only, and let the SIEM read them from each project across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: Organization-level aggregated sinks capture logs from all child projects and can route them to BigQuery and to Pub/Sub for external systems.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-project sinks don't scale and Cloud Storage alone doesn't feed a SIEM, dashboards don't export logs, and enabling log types doesn't route them.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Application logs for a project must be retained for two years and analyzed with SQL directly in Cloud Logging, while other logs keep the default retention. What should the engineer configure?
options: Increase the `_Default` bucket retention to two years and use Logs Explorer in Azure.
Change the `_Required` bucket retention to two years and query it with SQL as needed.
Export the application logs to a Filestore share and analyze them there.
Create a log bucket with two-year retention and Log Analytics, plus a routing sink.
questions.correct_rationale: User-defined log buckets can have custom retention and Log Analytics for SQL queries, and sinks route specific logs to them.
questions.distractor_summary: Changing `_Default` would affect all logs, `_Required` retention isn't configurable, and Filestore isn't a logging destination.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Cloud Monitoring shows CPU utilization for Compute Engine VMs but not memory usage or disk space utilization, and Nginx access logs from the VMs aren't in Cloud Logging. What should the engineer do?
options: Enable VPC Flow Logs for the subnet and read the memory data in the logs in that case.
Increase the machine type of the VMs so that they report memory usage.
Install the Ops Agent on the VMs and configure it to collect the Nginx logs.
Create an uptime check for each of the VMs and chart the results.
questions.correct_rationale: The Ops Agent collects guest-level metrics such as memory and disk usage, plus application logs such as Nginx logs.
questions.distractor_summary: Flow logs capture network data, machine type doesn't add telemetry, and uptime checks test external availability.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
