questions.question: A platform team runs applications on GKE that already expose Prometheus metrics and uses PromQL dashboards. It wants a fully managed, scalable Prometheus-compatible backend with long-term retention and doesn't want to operate Prometheus servers. What should the engineer use?
options: A self-managed Prometheus StatefulSet that has persistent disks for storage.
Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus, which collects from the pods.
Log-based metrics created from the logs of the application containers.
Uptime checks for every service that exposes metrics in the cluster.
questions.correct_rationale: Managed Service for Prometheus collects Prometheus metrics, supports PromQL, and stores data long-term without self-managed servers.
questions.distractor_summary: A self-managed StatefulSet adds operations work, and log-based metrics and uptime checks don't ingest Prometheus metrics.

questions.domain: 4. Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A production VM was deleted yesterday, and management wants to know who deleted it and when. No additional logging was configured in the project. Where should the engineer look?
options: Cloud Audit Logs Admin Activity logs, which are on by default and record deletions.
Data Access audit logs, which must be enabled first and then record who deleted it overall.
VPC Flow Logs for the subnet of the VM, which show the deleting user in every region.
The serial port output of the VM, which lists the deletion event.
questions.correct_rationale: Admin Activity audit logs are always on and capture API calls that modify resources, including who deleted the VM and when.
questions.distractor_summary: Data Access logs cover reading data and are off by default for most services, flow logs show network traffic, and serial output isn't available after deletion.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: During an access review, a manager asks for the complete list of principals and roles granted directly on project `payments-prod`. What should the engineer run?
options: `gcloud iam roles list --project=payments-prod`
`gcloud projects get-iam-policy payments-prod`
`gcloud iam service-accounts list --project=payments-prod`
`gcloud projects describe payments-prod` overall.
questions.correct_rationale: `get-iam-policy` returns the project's allow policy with all role bindings and members. `roles list` lists role definitions, `service-accounts list` lists only service accounts, and `describe` shows project metadata rather than IAM bindings.
questions.distractor_summary: Inherited bindings from folders or the organization appear on those resources' policies.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An engineer must grant `roles/logging.viewer` to `group:sre@example.com` on a project that has dozens of existing bindings managed by other teams. The engineer wants to avoid accidentally removing any existing access. What should the engineer run?
options: Edit the downloaded policy and run `gcloud projects set-iam-policy` without checking the etag.
Run `gcloud projects set-iam-policy` with a file holding only the new binding for the group.
Run `gcloud iam roles update roles/logging.viewer --add-members=sre@example.com` for the group.
Run `gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID --member=group:sre@example.com --role=roles/logging.viewer` for that binding.
questions.correct_rationale: `add-iam-policy-binding` adds a single binding while preserving the rest of the policy. `set-iam-policy` replaces the whole policy, which can wipe other bindings if the file is incomplete or stale, and predefined roles can't be edited to add members.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Data analysts must run queries against tables in the `sales` BigQuery dataset in project `analytics-prod`, but must not modify data or see other datasets. Query jobs should be billed to `analytics-prod`. Which roles should the engineer grant?
options: `roles/bigquery.dataViewer` on `sales`, and `roles/bigquery.jobUser` on `analytics-prod`.
`roles/bigquery.admin` on the `analytics-prod` project, which holds the `sales` dataset.
`roles/bigquery.dataEditor` on the `analytics-prod` project, which holds the `sales` dataset.
`roles/bigquery.user` on the organization, which contains the `analytics-prod` project.
questions.correct_rationale: Data Viewer on the dataset allows reading its tables, and Job User on the project allows running query jobs there.
questions.distractor_summary: Admin and Data Editor allow modifications, and organization-wide BigQuery User is far broader than needed.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A partner's application uploads daily files to the `partner-drop` Cloud Storage bucket. Security requires that the partner can create objects but can't list, read, overwrite, or delete any objects in the bucket. Which role should the engineer grant on the bucket?
options: `roles/storage.objectUser` on the bucket.
`roles/storage.objectAdmin` on the bucket.
`roles/storage.objectCreator` on the bucket.
`roles/storage.legacyBucketWriter` on the bucket.
questions.correct_rationale: Storage Object Creator allows creating objects without reading, listing, or deleting them.
questions.distractor_summary: Object User and Object Admin include read and delete permissions, and legacy roles are broader and not recommended.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An external auditor needs read access to a project for exactly two weeks, ending on June 30. The team wants the access to expire automatically without relying on someone remembering to remove it. What should the engineer configure?
options: A custom role whose description says that it expires after two weeks in Azure.
An IAM binding with a condition that allows access only before the end date.
A calendar reminder for an admin to remove the binding at the end of the two weeks.
An organization policy that expires on June 30 and removes the access overall.
questions.correct_rationale: IAM Conditions can restrict a binding based on time, so access stops automatically after the specified timestamp.
questions.distractor_summary: Role descriptions and calendar reminders don't enforce expiry, and organization policies constrain resource configuration rather than user access.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A development team should have `roles/storage.objectAdmin` only on buckets whose names start with `dev-` in a shared project that also contains production buckets. New `dev-` buckets are created frequently. What should the engineer configure?
options: Grant the role at the project level, so that it applies to all of the buckets throughout the organization.
Grant the role on each `dev-` bucket individually as each bucket is created throughout the organization overall.
Create a separate VPC for the development buckets and restrict access to it.
Grant it at the project level with an IAM Condition on names that start with `projects/_/buckets/dev-`.
questions.correct_rationale: Resource-name conditions can scope a project-level binding to buckets matching a prefix, automatically covering new buckets.
questions.distractor_summary: An unconditional project grant includes production buckets, per-bucket grants create ongoing work, and VPCs don't control Cloud Storage IAM.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An order service's service account must publish messages to the `orders` Pub/Sub topic, but must not publish to or read from any other topic or subscription in the project. What should the engineer do?
options: Grant `roles/pubsub.publisher` on the `orders` topic only.
Grant `roles/pubsub.editor` on the project that contains the `orders` topic.
Grant `roles/pubsub.publisher` on the project that contains the `orders` topic.
Grant `roles/pubsub.admin` on the `orders` topic to the service account.
questions.correct_rationale: Granting Publisher on the specific topic limits the service account to publishing there.
questions.distractor_summary: Project-level grants cover every topic, Editor allows modifications, and Admin allows managing the topic.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A security team needs to review IAM policies across all projects in the organization, including viewing role bindings and custom role definitions, but must not be able to change anything or read application data. Which role should the engineer grant at the organization level?
options: `roles/owner` on the organization.
`roles/viewer` on the organization.
`roles/iam.securityReviewer` on the organization.
`roles/iam.securityAdmin` on the organization.
questions.correct_rationale: Security Reviewer grants permission to list and get IAM policies and roles across resources without modification rights.
questions.distractor_summary: Owner and Security Admin allow changes, and Viewer grants read access to many resources' data, which is broader than needed.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A project management office wants its staff to see the organization's folders and projects to track which projects exist, without viewing resources such as VMs, buckets, or databases inside the projects. Which role should the engineer grant?
options: `roles/viewer` on the organization, granted to the PMO staff group.
`roles/browser` on the organization, granted to the PMO staff group.
`roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin` on the organization for the PMO group.
`roles/iam.securityReviewer` on the organization, granted to the PMO staff group.
questions.correct_rationale: Browser allows reading the resource hierarchy, including folders and projects, without access to resources inside projects.
questions.distractor_summary: Viewer allows reading most resources, Organization Admin allows management, and Security Reviewer focuses on IAM policies.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An audit found that 40 developers hold the Editor role on production projects. The CISO asks why this is a concern when developers need to deploy applications. What's the best explanation and recommendation?
options: Editor can't change IAM, so it is safe and no action is needed throughout the organization overall.
Replace Editor with Owner, which has stronger audit logging for each of the changes.
Remove all access and have developers email the operations team throughout the organization overall.
Editor is broad, so replace it with predefined roles for the services that developers deploy.
questions.correct_rationale: Basic roles such as Editor grant wide permissions across services, violating least privilege; predefined or custom roles limit access to what's needed.
questions.distractor_summary: Editor's inability to manage IAM doesn't make it low-risk, Owner is broader, and removing all access blocks legitimate work.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A company found that objects in some buckets were exposed through individual object ACLs that bypass its IAM reviews. It wants access to be controlled only through IAM at the bucket level. What should the engineer enable?
options: Uniform bucket-level access on each of the buckets.
Object Versioning on each of the buckets.
A locked retention policy on each of the buckets.
Customer-managed encryption keys on each bucket.
questions.correct_rationale: Uniform bucket-level access disables ACLs so that only bucket-level IAM controls access.
questions.distractor_summary: Versioning, retention policies, and CMEK don't change how access is granted.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A security analyst discovered that an unknown user was granted the Owner role on a project last week. The analyst needs to identify who made the change and when. Where should the engineer look?
options: VPC Flow Logs for the subnets in the project, filtered by the Owner role overall.
Cloud Monitoring metrics for the project, such as the IAM change count overall.
Cloud Audit Logs Admin Activity entries for `SetIamPolicy` on the project.
Billing export data in BigQuery, filtered by the last week for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: IAM policy changes are recorded in Admin Activity audit logs, including the principal who called `SetIamPolicy` and the timestamp.
questions.distractor_summary: Flow logs, metrics, and billing data don't record IAM changes.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An SRE team occasionally needs elevated production access during incidents. Security wants no standing privileged access, requires a justification and approval for each elevation, and wants access to expire automatically after a few hours. What should the engineer implement?
options: Grant Owner permanently to the SREs and review the access logs weekly.
Privileged Access Manager entitlements with temporary grants, a justification, and approval.
Share a break-glass service account key among the SREs and rotate it later.
Create a custom role and remove it by hand after each incident ends.
questions.correct_rationale: Privileged Access Manager provides just-in-time, time-bound privilege elevation with justification and optional approvals.
questions.distractor_summary: Standing Owner access violates the requirement, shared keys remove accountability, and manual removal is error-prone.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A Cloud Run service needs to read one database password stored in Secret Manager. The project contains 30 other secrets for different applications. What's the least-privilege configuration?
options: Grant `roles/secretmanager.admin` on the project to the service account.
Grant `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` on the project to the service account overall.
Store the password as a plain environment variable on the service instead.
Grant `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` on that one secret to the service account.
questions.correct_rationale: Secret Accessor on the single secret lets the service read only that secret's payload.
questions.distractor_summary: Project-level grants cover all 30 secrets, Admin allows management, and plain environment variables expose the password in configuration.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Two administrators downloaded a project's IAM policy at the same time, each added a different binding, and each ran `set-iam-policy`. The second update failed with a concurrency error. Why did this happen, and what should the second administrator do?
options: The policy's `etag` changed after the first update, so reread it, reapply the change, and set it again.
IAM allows only one administrator to change the policy of a project at a time throughout the organization.
The second administrator lacks the permission, so grant them the Owner role throughout the organization overall.
IAM policies can be changed only once per hour on each project throughout the organization in production.
questions.correct_rationale: IAM uses etags for optimistic concurrency, rejecting writes based on a stale policy so changes aren't silently overwritten.
questions.distractor_summary: There's no single-administrator or hourly limit, and the error isn't a permissions issue.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An engineer with `roles/logging.viewer` can see most logs in a project, but can't see Data Access audit logs needed for an investigation of who read sensitive Cloud Storage objects. What additional role does the engineer need?
options: `roles/logging.admin` on the project.
`roles/storage.objectViewer` on the project overall.
`roles/logging.privateLogViewer` on the project.
`roles/monitoring.viewer` on the project in Azure.
questions.correct_rationale: Data Access audit logs are private logs that require Private Logs Viewer in addition to standard log viewing.
questions.distractor_summary: Logging Admin grants more than needed, Object Viewer reads data rather than logs, and Monitoring Viewer covers metrics.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An application's service account needs to connect to a Cloud SQL instance, but must not be able to create, modify, or delete instances or databases. Which role should the engineer grant?
options: `roles/cloudsql.admin`
`roles/cloudsql.client`
`roles/cloudsql.editor`
`roles/cloudsql.viewer`
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud SQL Client allows connecting to instances (for example, through the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy or connectors) without management permissions.
questions.distractor_summary: Admin and Editor allow changes, and Viewer doesn't include connect permissions.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A data pipeline needs to write objects to the `pipeline-output` bucket. The project also contains buckets holding financial records. An engineer proposes granting `roles/storage.objectAdmin` at the project level to keep things simple. What should the engineer recommend instead?
options: Grant `roles/owner` to the pipeline for simplicity and consistency.
Make `pipeline-output` public-write so the pipeline can always write.
Grant `roles/storage.admin` at the organization level for the pipeline for the application.
Grant `roles/storage.objectCreator` or `objectUser` only on the `pipeline-output` bucket.
questions.correct_rationale: Granting the narrowest suitable role on the specific bucket follows least privilege and keeps the pipeline away from financial records.
questions.distractor_summary: Owner and organization-wide Storage Admin are far too broad, and public write access is insecure.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A team deploys a reporting application on Compute Engine using the Compute Engine default service account, which has the Editor role on the project. Security wants the application to have only the permissions it needs to read one bucket. What should the engineer do?
options: Create a dedicated service account with `roles/storage.objectViewer` on the bucket and attach it to the VM.
Keep the default service account and restrict its access scopes to read-only storage.
Remove the Editor role from the default service account in every project.
Create a service account key for the default service account and keep it on the VM.
questions.correct_rationale: A dedicated, narrowly scoped service account per workload follows least privilege.
questions.distractor_summary: Access scopes are a legacy mechanism that doesn't replace IAM least privilege, removing Editor from the default account everywhere may break other workloads, and keys add risk.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A developer has `roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1` on a project and tries to create a VM that runs as `reports-sa@project.iam.gserviceaccount.com`. The creation fails with a permission error related to the service account. What must be granted?
options: `roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin` on the project to the developer.
`roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin` on `reports-sa` to the developer.
`roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` on `reports-sa` to the developer.
`roles/owner` on the project to the developer.
questions.correct_rationale: Attaching a service account to a resource requires the `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` permission, provided by Service Account User on that account.
questions.distractor_summary: Service Account Admin and Key Admin manage accounts and keys rather than granting use, and Owner is excessive.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A security team wants to stop new projects in the organization from automatically granting the Editor role to the Compute Engine and App Engine default service accounts. What should the engineer configure?
options: An organization-wide IAM deny policy that covers the whole Editor role.
A Cloud Function that strips Editor from every new default service account.
Delete default service accounts everywhere and recreate them without roles.
Enforce the `constraints/iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts` constraint as an organization policy.
questions.correct_rationale: This boolean constraint prevents default service accounts from receiving the Editor role automatically when they're created.
questions.distractor_summary: Deny policies don't prevent the grant, a cleanup function is reactive, and deleting default accounts can break services that depend on them.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A VM runs as a custom service account that has `roles/bigquery.dataEditor` on a dataset. The VM was created with default access scopes, and the application receives "insufficient authentication scopes" errors when writing to BigQuery. What should the engineer do?
options: Grant the service account `roles/owner` on the project to fix it at that point in the project.
Stop the VM, set its access scope to `cloud-platform`, and let IAM roles control access.
Create a service account key and use it in the application code.
Enable the BigQuery API again in the project and restart the VM.
questions.correct_rationale: Access scopes limit OAuth tokens for the VM's service account, and default scopes don't include BigQuery write, so Google recommends the `cloud-platform` scope with IAM controlling access.
questions.distractor_summary: More IAM roles don't bypass scopes, keys add risk, and the API is already enabled.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An administrator needs to run gcloud commands with the permissions of the `deploy-sa` service account to test a deployment pipeline, without downloading any keys. What should the administrator do?
options: Get `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` on `deploy-sa` and use the `--impersonate-service-account` flag.
Create a key for `deploy-sa` and activate it with `gcloud auth activate-service-account`.
Grant the administrator the same roles that `deploy-sa` holds on the project.
Log in to the console as `deploy-sa` with a password that an owner resets.
questions.correct_rationale: Impersonation with Token Creator issues short-lived credentials for the service account without keys.
questions.distractor_summary: Key files are a security risk, duplicating roles doesn't test the service account itself, and service accounts don't have passwords for console login.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A scheduled script running under a user's identity must call an API as a service account for only a few minutes per run. Security wants credentials that expire quickly and are never written to disk. What should the engineer use?
options: A service account key that has a one-year expiration date throughout the organization in Azure.
The service account's email address and a shared password for the script across the subscriptions.
Short-lived access tokens from the IAM Service Account Credentials API through impersonation.
The Compute Engine default service account used on the laptop throughout the organization overall.
questions.correct_rationale: The Service Account Credentials API issues short-lived tokens (by default an hour or less) to authorized callers, without persistent keys.
questions.distractor_summary: Long-lived keys persist on disk, service accounts don't use passwords, and the default service account isn't available on laptops.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A security review found hundreds of long-lived service account keys in code repositories. The company wants to prevent anyone in the organization from creating new service account keys going forward. What should the engineer configure?
options: A conditional IAM binding restricting Service Account Key Administrators.
Rotate every existing key monthly, alerting whenever new keys appear.
Disable the Identity and Access Management API throughout the organization.
Enforce the organization policy constraint `constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` for all.
questions.correct_rationale: This constraint blocks creation of user-managed service account keys across the scope where it's enforced.
questions.distractor_summary: Conditions on roles don't block other principals with key permissions, rotation doesn't prevent creation, and disabling the IAM API breaks core functionality.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A legacy on-premises application that can't use workload identity federation requires a service account key. Security accepts this exception but wants risk minimized. What should the engineer do?
options: Embed the key in the application source code for reliability and speed.
Grant minimal roles, store the key in a secrets manager, rotate it often, and monitor its use.
Share the key with the whole engineering team so anyone can troubleshoot.
Grant the service account Owner so that the application never fails.
questions.correct_rationale: When keys can't be avoided, least-privilege roles, secure storage, regular rotation, and usage monitoring reduce risk.
questions.distractor_summary: Embedding keys in code, sharing them widely, and granting Owner all increase the impact of a leak.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A company deploys to Google Cloud from GitHub Actions. It currently stores a service account key as a GitHub secret. Security wants to eliminate keys while keeping automated deployments. What should the engineer configure?
options: Workload Identity Federation with a GitHub OIDC provider, so the workflow impersonates a service account.
A new service account key that is rotated weekly and stored in GitHub.
Grant the Owner role to the GitHub organization email address for deployments.
Use a developer personal credentials in GitHub for all of the deployments.
questions.correct_rationale: Workload Identity Federation lets external workloads exchange their OIDC tokens for short-lived Google Cloud credentials without keys.
questions.distractor_summary: Rotated keys are still keys, a GitHub organization isn't a Google identity that can receive roles this way, and personal credentials violate security practices.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An application running on Amazon EC2 needs to write data to a Cloud Storage bucket. The company doesn't want to store Google Cloud service account keys in AWS. What should the engineer set up?
options: Make the bucket public-write so that the EC2 instance can upload throughout the organization in every region.
Copy a service account key to each of the EC2 instances throughout the organization across the subscriptions.
Workload Identity Federation with an AWS provider, so the instance's AWS role gets short-lived credentials.
Create a Cloud Identity user for the EC2 instance and share its password throughout the organization overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Workload Identity Federation supports AWS as an identity provider, so AWS workloads can obtain short-lived Google credentials without keys.
questions.distractor_summary: Public write access is insecure, keys on instances are the risk to avoid, and user accounts aren't meant for workloads.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An engineer believes the service account `old-etl-sa` is no longer used and wants to remove it, but isn't completely sure. What is the safest approach?
options: Delete the service account immediately, even though it can't be restored overall.
Remove all of its roles and delete its keys at once to be safe.
Rename the service account and wait to see what breaks in the logs by default.
Disable it first, watch for failures, and delete it later if nothing breaks.
questions.correct_rationale: Disabling a service account stops it from authenticating while keeping it recoverable, so dependencies can be discovered before deletion; deleted accounts can also be undeleted within a limited window.
questions.distractor_summary: Immediate deletion or stripping roles is riskier, and service accounts can't be renamed.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: While cleaning up IAM, an engineer notices accounts such as `service-123456789@compute-system.iam.gserviceaccount.com` with roles on the project that nobody on the team created. The engineer plans to remove them. What should the engineer know?
options: They are leftover accounts from deleted users, so removing them is safe.
They are Google-managed service agents, and removing their roles can break those services.
They are compromised accounts, so they should be deleted immediately.
They are user-managed service accounts created by default, so replace them.
questions.correct_rationale: Service agents are Google-managed service accounts that services use to access resources on your behalf, and their role grants are required for those services to work.
questions.distractor_summary: They aren't user leftovers, compromised accounts, or user-managed accounts.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A team tries to attach a service account from the `shared-identities` project to a VM in the `app-prod` project. The user has Service Account User on that service account, but the operation fails with an organization policy error. What's the cause?
options: The organization enforces `constraints/iam.disableCrossProjectServiceAccountUsage` on every project.
Service accounts are never attachable to resources inside different projects.
The virtual machine must be stopped before attachment is attempted.
The service account requires an external key to be created first.
questions.correct_rationale: This constraint, enforced by default in many organizations, blocks attaching service accounts to resources in other projects until it's relaxed for the relevant projects.
questions.distractor_summary: Cross-project use is otherwise supported, VM state isn't relevant, and keys aren't involved.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A developer is testing code locally that uses Google Cloud client libraries and wants the libraries to authenticate automatically using their own user credentials, without downloading any service account keys. What should the developer run?
options: Run `gcloud auth login` only, and then run the application again.
Run `gcloud iam service-accounts keys create key.json` for the developer.
Run `gcloud auth application-default login` to create local credentials.
Run `gcloud config set account service-account@project.iam.gserviceaccount.com` for the app.
questions.correct_rationale: `application-default login` sets up Application Default Credentials that client libraries use automatically. `gcloud auth login` authorizes the gcloud CLI itself, creating keys is what should be avoided, and setting the gcloud account doesn't configure client library credentials.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A project contains 20 service accounts, including a highly privileged `billing-export-sa`. A deployment team needs to attach only `web-sa` to Cloud Run services. The proposal is to grant Service Account User at the project level. What should the engineer do instead?
options: Grant Service Account Admin on the project to the deployment team.
Grant Service Account User at the project level to the deployment team, as proposed.
Grant Owner on the project to the deployment team for the deployments.
Grant Service Account User on the `web-sa` service account only.
questions.correct_rationale: Service accounts are also resources, so Service Account User can be granted on a single account, preventing the team from acting as privileged accounts like `billing-export-sa`. A project-level grant allows acting as all 20 accounts, and Admin or Owner is far broader.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A company has 12 Cloud Run services that all run as a single shared service account with permissions for every database, bucket, and topic they collectively need. A vulnerability in one service could expose all resources. What should the engineer recommend?
options: Grant the shared service account fewer roles and accept that some calls fail in the project.
Create a dedicated service account for each service with only the roles that it needs.
Use the Compute Engine default service account for all of the services.
Use a service account key for each of the services and rotate it.
questions.correct_rationale: A dedicated identity per workload limits the blast radius of a compromise and allows least-privilege grants per service.
questions.distractor_summary: Removing needed roles breaks services, the default service account is typically over-privileged, and keys add risk without improving isolation.

questions.domain: 5. Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A security team wants to find service accounts and service account keys that haven't been used in the last 90 days so they can be disabled or deleted. What should the engineer use?
options: Policy Analyzer activity analysis and Recommender service account insights for last authentication.
VPC Flow Logs for the subnets that the service accounts use, over 90 days.
Cloud Billing reports that list the costs for each service account.
The Cloud Monitoring uptime check list for each project in the organization.
questions.correct_rationale: Policy Analyzer activity analysis and Recommender insights show when service accounts and keys last authenticated, identifying unused ones.
questions.distractor_summary: Flow logs, billing reports, and uptime checks don't track authentication activity.
